etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Portuguese inhame and Spanish ñame, likely from Wolof ñàmbi (“cassava”) or a related word. The term was spelled yam as early as 1657.

definitions.definition: Any climbing vine of the genus Dioscorea in the Eastern and Western hemispheres, usually cultivated.
The edible, starchy, tuberous root of that plant, a tropical staple food.

quote.citation: 1958, Chinua Achebe, chapter 4, in Things Fall Apart, New York: Astor-Honor, published 1959, part 1, page 34:
quote.text: Inwardly Okonkwo knew that the boys were still too young to understand fully the difficult art of preparing seed-yams. But he thought that one could not begin too early. Yam stood for manliness, and he who could feed his family on yams from one harvest to another was a very great man indeed.

definitions.definition: (US) A sweet potato; a tuber from the species Ipomoea batatas.
(New Zealand) An oca; a tuber from the species Oxalis tuberosa.
An orange-brown colour, like the flesh of the yam. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Alternative form of hjem. Likely caused by influence from Old Norse heim (“home, homewards”), the accusative form of heimr (“abode, world, land”), from Proto-Germanic *haimaz. More at home.

quote.citation: 1904, Carrie Hunt Latta, “The Last Day of Schol”, in The Reader Magazine‎[1], volume IV, Indianopolis: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, page 291:
quote.text: “Stay, jailer, stay, and hear my woe,” repeating again and again, very softly, the line at the end of each stanza, “I am not mad, I am not mad.” Except she sang it: “I yam not mad, I yam not mad.”

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Ultimately from Fula nyaamude (“to eat”) or a cognate Fula-Wolof term.

quote.citation: 2016, Zadie Smith, Swing Time, New York, N.Y.: Penguin Press, →ISBN, page 78:
quote.text: “If I was that snake I’d just open my jaw and yam that fool up in one bite!”

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Apparently a variation of jam (“dunk”, verb).

definitions.definition: (especially basketball) To dunk on; to beat humiliatingly.
